landmarks.name: Tarrant County Courthouse
landmarks.info: Pink Texas granite, 1895, on the bluff over the Trinity where Camp Worth stood in 1849: the county built it so grand that the voters threw out the commissioners who paid for it. Main Street runs south from its steps to the Water Gardens.

landmarks.name: Bass Performance Hall
landmarks.info: 1998, built with private money and no public funds: a limestone hall for the symphony, the opera and the Van Cliburn competition, its two twelve-metre angels blowing their trumpets from the front.

landmarks.name: Sundance Square Plaza
landmarks.info: The square at the heart of downtown, opened in 2013 where there were parking lots: four great shade umbrellas, fountains to run through, and a Christmas tree in December. Named for the Sundance Kid, who hid out in Hell's Half Acre with Butch Cassidy.

landmarks.name: The Chisholm Trail mural
landmarks.info: Richard Haas's trompe-l'oeil of 1985 on the Jett Building: the cattle drive crossing the Trinity on the Chisholm Trail, which came through Fort Worth on its way from Texas to the Kansas railheads.
landmarks._at: on the wall across 4th Street from the plaza, facing it; the Jett Building is not named on the map

landmarks.name: Fort Worth Water Gardens
landmarks.info: Philip Johnson's, 1974: a 'cooling oasis in a concrete jungle'. The Active Pool pours down terraces of concrete into a square pit you can walk down into; the Quiet Pool is still, and the Aerating Pool's jets dance.

landmarks.name: Kimbell Art Museum
landmarks.info: Louis Kahn's, 1972, perhaps the finest museum building in America: sixteen cycloid vaults of concrete, each open along its crown so that daylight runs down the silver underside of the vault onto the paintings.
landmarks._face: the vaults run north and south (the footprint is 97 m that way) and the porticoes open west onto the lawn: face 180 turns the model's rows north-south with its porticoes (its -x end) to the west

landmarks.name: Modern Art Museum of Fort Worth
replace: Modern Art Museum of Fort Worth
landmarks.info: Tadao Ando's, 2002: five long glass-and-concrete pavilions standing in a reflecting pond under flat roofs on Y-shaped columns, across the street from the Kimbell.

landmarks.name: Pioneer Tower
landmarks.info: The Art Deco tower of the Will Rogers Memorial Center, 1936, built for the Texas Centennial between the coliseum and the auditorium. The Fort Worth Stock Show and Rodeo is held round it every January.

landmarks.name: Livestock Exchange Building
landmarks.info: 1902, the 'Wall Street of the West': the cattle trading offices of the Fort Worth Stockyards, Mission Revival in white stucco under red tile. More than a million head a year were sold here at the market's height.

landmarks.name: Cowtown Coliseum
landmarks.info: 1908: the world's first indoor rodeo was held here in 1918, and the first live radio broadcast of one. Enrico Caruso sang here; so did Elvis. Rodeo every weekend.

landmarks.name: Billy Bob's Texas
landmarks.info: The world's largest honky-tonk, in a cattle barn of 1910: a hundred thousand square feet, an arena for live bull riding, and room for six thousand.

landmarks.name: Fort Worth Stockyards sign
landmarks.info: Over East Exchange Avenue at North Main Street: the arch you drive under into the Stockyards National Historic District.

landmarks.name: Burnett Plaza
landmarks.info: 567 ft (173 m), 1983: the tallest building in Fort Worth, dark glass on a granite base, named for Samuel Burk Burnett, the rancher whose fortune built much of downtown.

landmarks.name: Bank of America Tower
landmarks.info: City Center Tower II, 1984, 167 m: the Bass brothers' towers, their tops stepped back in notches, the pair that defines the skyline from the Trinity.

landmarks.name: 777 Main
landmarks.info: Formerly Carter Burgess Plaza and the Continental Plaza, 1982: 160 m of granite and glass.

landmarks.name: Fort Worth Central Station
landmarks.info: The transit hub: TEXRail to DFW Airport and the Trinity Railway Express to Dallas, Amtrak's Texas Eagle and Heartland Flyer, and the buses.

landmarks.name: Texas and Pacific Terminal
landmarks.info: 1931, Art Deco, the T&P Railway's passenger station and its office block; the trains of TEXRail and the TRE still stop at its platforms.

landmarks.name: Dickies Arena
landmarks.info: 2019, home of the Stock Show's rodeo: a domed arena in a Spanish Colonial and Art Deco dress to match the Will Rogers buildings round it.

landmarks.name: Robert Carr Chapel
landmarks.info: TCU's chapel, 1953, its white steeple over the campus quadrangle.
